strengths: Identifies a genuine and well-motivated gap: no existing benchmark systematically evaluates MLLMs' ability to judge visualization quality (fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics), and Table 1 clearly positions the work against related benchmarks.

The benchmark is substantial and diverse: 3,090 real-world samples across 32 chart subtypes spanning single visualizations, multi-visualizations, and dashboards, with a documented multi-stage collection pipeline (crawling, pHash dedup, LLM filtering, stratified sampling) described in detail.

The three-stage annotation workflow (crowdsourcing with validation checks, algorithmic disagreement analysis, expert adjudication) is unusually thorough for a benchmark of this type, and the appendices provide extensive reproducibility detail (prompts, interfaces, hyperparameters).

The evaluation of seven models including GPT-5 yields interesting findings: hierarchical capability structure across dimensions, systematic score-inflation/conservatism biases, and degradation on dashboards, supported by both quantitative (MAE/MSE/correlation) and qualitative case studies.
The data-scaling analysis (logarithmic correlation growth, exponential error decay) provides practically useful guidance for annotation budgets.

VisJudge with GRPO fine-tuning demonstrates clear gains over all baselines (MAE 0.442, correlation 0.681), validating the benchmark as a training resource, and the distribution analysis showing near-human mean alignment (μ=3.11 vs 3.13) is convincing evidence of bias correction.
weaknesses: Potential circularity/contamination: VisJudge is trained on 70% of the benchmark and evaluated on the remaining 20%, and the benchmark is presented simultaneously as a training resource and an evaluation set. Future model comparisons on VisJudge-Bench will be confounded because the released benchmark is the authors' own training set; no external validation set or cross-benchmark generalization test is provided.

Ground-truth reliability is under-validated. The 'human experts' are largely crowdsourced annotators ($10/hr, Bachelor's degree) with only three in-house experts for adjudication. No inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Krippendorff's alpha, human-human correlation) are reported, so the apparent model-human gap (best correlation 0.48) cannot be distinguished from annotation noise; the effective upper bound on achievable correlation is unknown.

The adaptive question generation and metadata extraction rely on GPT-4o, injecting LLM biases into the evaluation rubrics themselves; the sensitivity of the ground truth to this design choice is not ablated.

The VisJudge contribution lacks key ablations: no comparison against supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of the same base model on the same data, no analysis of the reward function weights, and no statistical significance testing for the improvements (19.8% MAE reduction is modest in absolute terms: 0.551 → 0.442).

The web-crawled corpus is biased by construction: search queries deliberately include quality modifiers ('poor,' 'confusing,' 'professional'), which may produce visually distinctive low/high-quality clusters that a fine-tuned model can exploit, inflating the apparent benefit of training on in-distribution data.

No fine-tuned baselines among the compared models (all baselines are off-the-shelf), so the headline improvement partially reflects task-specific training rather than a like-for-like comparison; also, only one base model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) is tested for the fine-tuning recipe.
Ethics/copyright handling is thin: visualizations are scraped from the web and redistributed, and the ethics statement acknowledges but does not resolve licensing concerns for the 3,090 images.

Some framing is overstated: 'first comprehensive benchmark' claims compete with closely related concurrent work (e.g., VIS-Shepherd), and the improvement percentages (58.7% correlation improvement) are computed relative to a weak absolute baseline.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: no existing benchmark systematically measures MLLM judgment of visualization quality across fidelity, expressiveness, and aesthetics; Table 1 positioning against ChartQA/ChartInsights/VisEval/Vis-Shepherd is reasonable and well-motivated.

The benchmark construction effort is substantial: 3,090 samples spanning 32 chart types across single visualizations, multi-visualizations, and dashboards, with a documented multi-stage collection, deduplication, and filtering pipeline (300k images down to 3,090).

The three-stage annotation workflow (crowdsourced annotation, algorithmic conflict detection, expert adjudication) is thoughtfully designed and described in unusual detail, including interfaces and candidate-resolution strategies.

The evaluation is broad: seven MLLMs including frontier models (GPT-5, Claude-4-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro), fine-grained per-dimension analysis (MAE/MSE/correlation), score-distribution bias analysis, complexity analysis, qualitative case studies, and a data-scaling study.
Reproducibility appears good: prompts, hyperparameters, reward functions, splits, and dataset statistics are documented in appendices, and the benchmark is stated to be released.
weaknesses: Ground-truth reliability is asserted but never quantified: no inter-annotator agreement statistics (Krippendorff's alpha, ICC, or even pairwise agreement) are reported for the crowdsourced scores, and the three 'experts' in Stage 3 are described only as having 'visualization analysis experience' with no stated credentials. Without a human-human agreement ceiling, it is impossible to interpret absolute values like correlation 0.482 for GPT-5 or 0.681 for VisJudge; the model may already be near the human-agreement ceiling.

A self-referential evaluation design weakens the central claims: VisJudge is trained on 70% of VISJUDGE-BENCH and evaluated on the test split of the same benchmark, generated with the same GPT-4o-authored question templates and scoring rubrics used at test time. The 19.8% MAE reduction and 58.7% correlation gain may substantially reflect fitting the benchmark's rubric conventions and distribution rather than genuine improvement in evaluation capability; no external, out-of-distribution validation is provided.

The headline comparison is inconsistent and favors the authors' model: the abstract compares VisJudge against GPT-5 for correlation, but Table 3 shows GPT-4o achieves higher correlation (0.482), making the claimed improvement smaller (0.482 to 0.681, still modest on a 1-5 scale). Absolute improvements in MAE (~0.11 on a 1-5 scale) are small, and no statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or variance across the three evaluation runs are reported.

The ground truth itself depends on LLM-generated questions and metadata: GPT-4o 'adaptive question generation' and metadata extraction inject potential noise and bias into the evaluation questions that both human annotators and tested models see, and the impact of this on label quality is never analyzed.

Novelty is incremental: the core recipe (collect images, define rubric dimensions, crowdsource + adjudicate scores, evaluate MLLMs as judges, fine-tune a small model with GRPO) closely follows established MLLM-as-a-judge and benchmark-construction patterns (e.g., AVA, ArtiMuse, Vis-Shepherd), and the 'Fidelity, Expressiveness, Aesthetics' framing is borrowed from translation theory without strong justification that these are the right or sufficient dimensions.

Some analyses overreach: the 'predictable scaling laws' claim is based on a single training run with one data-scale sweep of one 7B model on one benchmark, with R^2 values fitted to six points; 'near-perfect alignment' with human scoring (mu = 3.11 vs 3.13) reflects matching a mean, not necessarily improved judgment quality.

Benchmark balance issues: the test set is only 648 samples; some subtypes are extremely sparse (Word Cloud, Violin Plot n=1 in the full set; 'Other Dashboard' n=1 in test), making per-type conclusions unreliable, and the corpus skews toward Western/English web sources without discussion of cultural bias despite the acknowledged subjectivity of aesthetics.

The stated ethics/compensation ($10/hour for a 30-60 minute, cognitively demanding 90-question task) raises concern about annotator motivation and quality, further underscoring the need for the missing reliability statistics.

strengths: Addresses a genuine research gap: there is no systematic benchmark for evaluating MLLMs' ability to judge visualization quality, and the paper clearly differentiates itself from chart-QA, aesthetic-assessment, and NL2VIS benchmarks (Table 1).

Substantial and well-documented data curation effort: 3,090 real-world samples spanning single visualizations, multi-view charts, and dashboards across 32 subtypes, with a multi-stage filtering pipeline (perceptual-hash dedup, LLM-based classification, stratified sampling) and a three-stage annotation workflow with validation checks, disagreement detection, and expert adjudication.

Comprehensive evaluation protocol: seven representative models including GPT-5, MAE/MSE/Pearson correlation reported per sub-dimension, three-run averaging, score-distribution bias analysis (Figure 4), complexity-stratified analysis (Figure 5), qualitative case studies, and a data-scaling study (Figure 8).

VisJudge provides meaningful improvements over the strongest baselines (MAE 0.551→0.442; correlation 0.429→0.681 vs GPT-5), and the case studies (Figures 6-7, 21-25) concretely illustrate systematic failure modes such as score inflation and conservatism.
Transparent reporting of annotation procedures, prompts, reward functions, and hyperparameters in the appendix supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Missing human-human agreement baseline. The paper's central claim is that models fall short of 'human experts,' but the inter-annotator correlation/MAE among the three crowdsourced annotators (or between annotators and the expert panel) is never reported. Without this ceiling, it is impossible to interpret whether GPT-5's 0.429 correlation represents a large or small gap, or whether VisJudge's 0.681 merely matches annotator noise. This is the most significant methodological omission.

Potential circularity and overfitting concerns: VisJudge is trained on the same corpus, the same six-dimensional rubric, and the same annotation style as the test set, so its improvement may partly reflect learning annotator biases rather than genuine evaluation capability. There is no out-of-distribution validation (e.g., a held-out dataset annotated independently, or testing generalization to charts from a different source), yet the paper draws the broad conclusion that 'domain-specific fine-tuning is necessary.'

Misleading terminology: the abstract claims samples are 'expert-annotated,' but Section 3.1.3 reveals the primary annotations come from crowdsourced workers (screened, but not experts), with expert review applied mainly to disputed samples. This should be stated accurately.

Limited novelty in methodology: the technical contribution of VisJudge is a fairly standard recipe (Qwen2.5-VL-7B + LoRA + GRPO with a simple accuracy/format reward). There is no ablation comparing GRPO against plain SFT, no analysis of reward weighting (0.9/0.1 is chosen without justification), and no comparison with other adaptation strategies, weakening the claim that the proposed approach itself is a contribution rather than an expected consequence of fine-tuning on the benchmark.

Some internal inconsistencies and loose claims: the abstract reports a 58.7% correlation improvement over GPT-5 while Section 5.2.1 reports a 41.3% improvement over GPT-4o; 'hierarchical capability structure' claims (e.g., models perform better on Insight Discovery than Semantic Readability) cite average MAEs whose computation across models is not clearly defined; the 'Fidelity, Expressiveness, Aesthetics' framing borrowed from translation theory is loosely motivated for visualization.

Fidelity assessment is done from images alone without underlying data, meaning 'data fidelity' scores partly reflect annotator plausibility judgments rather than verifiable accuracy; the paper does not discuss this limitation.

Statistical rigor: no significance tests or confidence intervals on the correlation/MAE differences; the test set is a single 648-sample split; temperature 0.8 with three-run averaging mitigates but does not eliminate variance concerns.

The evaluation questions and rubrics were generated with GPT-4o and given identically to all models, so the benchmark measures instruction-following on a specific rubric as much as evaluation ability; the impact of rubric phrasing is not analyzed.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research gap: the paper convincingly argues that existing chart-understanding, NL2VIS, and natural-image aesthetics benchmarks do not measure MLLMs' ability to *judge* holistic visualization quality, and Table 1 clearly positions VisJudge-Bench against prior work.

Substantial benchmark construction effort: 3,090 samples spanning single charts, multi-view compositions, and dashboards across 32 subtypes, with a multi-stage pipeline (web crawling at 300k scale, hash dedup, LLM filtering, stratified sampling) and a rigorous three-stage annotation workflow (crowd annotation with embedded validation checks, algorithmic conflict resolution, expert adjudication). The appendix thoroughly documents statistics, score distributions, and annotator quality analyses (e.g., crowd-crowd and crowd-expert MAE).

Broad and informative evaluation: 12 representative MLLMs including GPT-5, Claude-4, and Gemini-2.5, evaluated with MAE/MSE/correlation across six sub-dimensions, plus distribution-shift analysis (score inflation, score concentration) and complexity analysis. The fine-tuning is validated across four architectures (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, LLaVA) with consistent gains, supporting cross-architecture generality.

Practical impact demonstrated beyond the benchmark: integrating VisJudge as feedback in MatPlotAgent and as a reward model in HAIChart shows consistent improvements in OOD settings, and the data-scaling analysis (logarithmic correlation growth, exponential error decay) offers useful deployment guidance.
Honest limitations section and ethics statement; commitment to public release of data, annotations, and model weights supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Circularity risk in the headline claims: VisJudge is fine-tuned on 70% of VisJudge-Bench and then evaluated on its test split, so the '23.9% MAE reduction over GPT-5' partly reflects in-distribution fine-tuning advantage rather than a fundamental capability gain. The paper would benefit from a stronger held-out/external evaluation or explicit discussion; GPT-5 is evaluated zero-shot on the same distribution, making the comparison somewhat asymmetric.

The gold-standard labels are inherently noisy and subjective, especially for aesthetics: reported crowd-crowd MAE is 0.64–0.70 and crowd-expert MAE 0.54–0.59. VisJudge's MAE of 0.421 being *below* inter-annotator agreement suggests models may partly be learning systematic annotation biases (or that MAE against expert labels is not a meaningful noise floor), which weakens the significance of absolute MAE numbers.

The ML methodology is fairly standard (LoRA + GRPO with an accuracy/format reward); there are no ablations comparing GRPO against simple SFT, no comparison against prompt-engineering or calibration-based bias mitigation baselines (e.g., score distribution correction), so the specific value of the RL approach is unverified.

Data fidelity assessment is limited to visual-level inspection since source data is unavailable for web-collected charts; the 'Fidelity' dimension may therefore conflate presentation quality with actual data truthfulness, and the average fidelity MAE (~1.0) is surprisingly high yet described qualitatively as 'relatively well' performance — the analysis framing is inconsistent.

The MatPlotAgent experiments use GPT-4o as the automatic quality judge (0–100), which is itself subject to the biases documented in the paper; using an MLLM judge to validate a judge model introduces an additional layer of circularity.

Annotation pool is heavily US-based (88.7%) with limited demographic diversity, which the authors acknowledge; aesthetic judgments in particular are culture-dependent, limiting generalizability of the benchmark.

Some positioning elements are incremental: the fine-tuned model contribution is a natural follow-up to the benchmark, and prior work such as Vis-Shepherd already constructs LLM-based visualization critics, narrowing the claimed novelty.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: there is no established benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of visualization quality (fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics), in contrast to chart QA and NL2VIS benchmarks (clearly positioned in Table 1).

Substantial data construction effort: 3,090 expert-adjudicated samples across 32 chart types, three visualization categories, six sub-dimensions, with a documented multi-stage crowdsourcing workflow, embedded validation checks, and quality-control analysis (crowd-crowd and crowd-expert MAE).
Broad evaluation across 12 closed- and open-source MLLMs including GPT-5, with analyses of score-distribution biases (inflation, concentration) that are diagnostically useful.
Validation beyond the benchmark itself: integration as feedback/reward into MatPlotAgent and HAIChart, and cross-architecture fine-tuning experiments (four backbones), plus a data-scaling analysis.
Comprehensive appendices (prompts, annotation interface, hyperparameters) supporting reproducibility, with a stated plan to release data and model weights.
weaknesses: Circularity/shortcut concern for the headline claim: VISJUDGE is fine-tuned on the same distribution, questions, and rubric as the test split, so the reported gains (MAE 0.553→0.421, correlation 0.482→0.687) may largely reflect learning the crowd/expert scoring distribution (e.g., matching the human mean μ≈3.13 and correction of score inflation) rather than genuinely better quality judgment. No held-out rubric, question style, or source-distribution transfer experiment for the core benchmark metric is provided to rule this out.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: the text claims models 'perform relatively well on Fidelity (average MAE 1.006)' but simultaneously 'struggle significantly with Aesthetics (MAE around 0.755)' — the reported numbers say the opposite (Fidelity MAE is the worst in Table 3). Similar loose claims (e.g., 'near-perfect alignment' for μ=3.11) overstate the evidence.

The 'fine-tuning vs. GPT-5' headline comparisons (23.9% MAE reduction, 60.5% correlation improvement) compare a domain-specialized model against a general-purpose model on the specialist's own training rubric — a comparison that is expected to favor the fine-tuned model and is not equally informative as a capability claim.

Test set is only 648 samples; no statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or variance estimates across the three inference runs are reported, so the claimed improvements across many close model rankings are not statistically substantiated.

Benchmark construction depends heavily on GPT-4o for filtering, classification, metadata extraction, and adaptive question rewriting; GPT-4o-injected biases in question phrasing and scoring criteria are not analyzed, and could favor models stylistically similar to GPT-4o.

Human annotation noise floor is comparable to the reported model improvements: crowd-crowd MAE is 0.64–0.70, yet the celebrated gap closure is on the order of 0.1 MAE, so practical significance is unclear.

Some sub-dimensions are conceptually shaky (e.g., 'Design Style' scores rewarding 'innovation/uniqueness' of web-scraped charts), and only three 'experts' with unspecified visualization-analysis credentials adjudicate all 3,090 samples.

Novelty is moderate: the recipe (build a benchmark via crowdsourcing + LLM question generation, then LoRA/GRPO fine-tune a judge model) is standard; the closest related work (VisEval, VIS-Shepherd) is differentiated mainly by the added aesthetics dimensions. The 'mathematical scaling law' framing of Figure 8 (log/exponential fits on R²≈0.68–0.98 over a limited range) is over-interpreted.

Missing baselines/ablations for the benchmark design: no comparison against simpler judge protocols (e.g., generic rubric without adaptive GPT-4o question rewriting), no inter-rater metrics like Krippendorff's alpha for the final gold scores, and no analysis of score-weighting choices for the aggregated overall score.

Annotator pool is ~89% U.S.-based with a $10/hr rate; aesthetic judgments across cultural backgrounds are acknowledged as a limitation but not addressed, which weakens the 'human expert' gold-standard claim for aesthetics dimensions.

strengths: Clear identification of a genuine research gap: no existing benchmark systematically measures MLLM capability as a 'visualization quality judge' across fidelity, expressiveness, and aesthetics; Table 1 effectively positions the work against chart-QA, NL2VIS, and natural-image aesthetics benchmarks.

Large-scale, well-documented benchmark construction: 3,090 real-world web-sourced samples across 32 chart subtypes (single vis, multi-vis, dashboards), with a three-stage annotation workflow (603 screened crowd annotators, disagreement-driven quality control, expert adjudication) and detailed inter-annotator reliability analysis in the appendix.

Comprehensive and well-organized evaluation: 12 MLLMs including frontier models, multi-metric analysis (MAE/MSE/correlation), score-distribution bias analysis revealing systematic score inflation, per-dimension breakdowns, and per-visualization-type complexity analysis.

The proposed VisJudge goes beyond a benchmark paper: consistent improvements across four different backbone architectures (3B-8B), scaling-law analysis of training data, and importantly two out-of-distribution real-world integrations (MatPlotAgent feedback and HAIChart reward) demonstrating practical utility, not just leaderboard gains.
Strong reproducibility posture: extensive appendices with prompts, annotation interfaces, scoring rubrics, hyperparameters, and a commitment to releasing data, annotations, and model weights.
weaknesses: Inherent subjectivity and possible rubric rigidity: aesthetic dimensions (design style, color harmony) are judged by LLM-generated questions with fixed 1-5 anchors; baseline correlations of ~0.1-0.3 on these dimensions may partly reflect ill-defined rubrics rather than pure model deficiency, and the ground truth is a small panel (3 experts) of unverified expertise.

Potential circularity/bias in benchmark construction: GPT-4o is used for classification, metadata extraction, and question/criterion rewriting, and the same question templates are then used to evaluate MLLMs (including GPT-4o itself); the paper does not measure how sensitive scores are to the LLM-generated phrasing of questions and scoring criteria.

Benchmark-train-test leakage concerns: VisJudge is fine-tuned on 70% of the same corpus and evaluated on the remaining 20% of the same distribution, so the headline 23.9% MAE reduction and 60.5% correlation gain overstate in-domain fit; OOD validation exists (MatPlotAgent/HAIChart) but uses weak or indirect evaluation protocols (e.g., GPT-4o as final judge, Hit@k against a possibly noisy recommendation ground truth).

Suspiciously strong fit to expert labels: the fine-tuned model's MAE (0.421) is lower than the reported crowd-expert MAE (0.545-0.585) and inter-annotator MAE (0.64-0.70), which raises the question of whether the model is learning genuine quality signals or expert-specific idiosyncrasies of a small labeling team; no test of generalization to an independent expert panel is provided.

Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple-comparison handling for the many per-dimension/per-type comparisons; some claims (e.g., 'logarithmic growth' / 'exponential decay' scaling laws) are fitted to few points on a single model and single epoch without error bars.

Possible contamination: images were web-crawled, so many charts likely appear in the training data of closed-source models (GPT-5, Gemini, Claude), which could inflate their apparent capability or distort gap conclusions; no decontamination analysis is discussed.

Minor inconsistencies/omissions: annotator compensation appears low for a 30-60 minute expert-leaning task; some claimed numbers (e.g., 'correlation with human 0.428' for GPT-5 vs 0.482 for GPT-4o in the abstract vs text) require careful cross-checking; the 'Fidelity/Expressiveness/Aesthetics' framing borrows translation-theory terminology somewhat loosely.
